rules.name: Arbitrary union of open sets
preconditions: Each set in the union is open in the same topology
rules.operation: Preserve openness under arbitrary unions.
examples: The union of open intervals in R is open
counterexamples: Replacing arbitrary union with arbitrary intersection is invalid in general

rules.name: Finite intersection of open sets
preconditions: Each set in the intersection is open in the same topology
rules.operation: Preserve openness under finite intersections.
examples: Intersection of two open intervals is open or empty, both open in the standard topology
counterexamples: Infinite intersection of open sets need not be open

rules.name: Closed set complement rule
rules.operation: Characterize closed sets by openness of complements.
examples: A closed interval in R has open complement
counterexamples: Treating openness and closedness as mutually exclusive in general is invalid

rules.name: Continuity by preimages of open sets
rules.output_form: continuous iff all open preimages are open
preconditions: A domain and codomain topology are fixed
rules.operation: Characterize continuity topologically through preimages of open sets.
examples: Polynomial maps are continuous in the usual topology on R
counterexamples: Checking only images of open sets does not characterize continuity in general

rules.name: Basis criterion for a topology
preconditions: The collection covers the space and satisfies local intersection refinement
rules.operation: Recognize when a collection of subsets generates a topology as a basis.
examples: Open intervals form a basis for the standard topology on R
counterexamples: A collection missing points of the space cannot be a basis for the whole space

rules.name: Compactness by open covers
preconditions: Compactness is interpreted through open covers
rules.operation: Use the finite-subcover property to characterize compactness.
examples: Closed interval [0,1] is compact in the standard topology on R
counterexamples: An open interval (0,1) is not compact in the standard topology on R

rules.name: Connectedness by no separation
rules.operation: Characterize connectedness through impossibility of separation into two disjoint nonempty open pieces.
examples: An interval in R is connected
counterexamples: A set split into two separated open pieces is disconnected

rules.name: Hausdorff separation rule
preconditions: The space is claimed to be Hausdorff
rules.operation: Separate distinct points by disjoint open neighborhoods.
examples: Standard Euclidean spaces are Hausdorff
counterexamples: A topology where distinct points cannot be separated by disjoint open sets is not Hausdorff

rules.name: Closure operator definition
rules.operation: Interpret closure as the intersection of all closed supersets of a set.
examples: Closure of an open interval in standard real topology adds its limit boundary points
counterexamples: Omitting boundary limit points from closure is invalid

rules.name: Interior operator definition
rules.operation: Interpret interior as the largest open set contained in a set.
examples: Interior of [0,1] in R is (0,1)
counterexamples: Including boundary points without an open neighborhood contained in A is invalid

rules.name: Boundary relation
rules.operation: Express boundary through closure and interior.
examples: Boundary of (0,1) in R is {0,1}
counterexamples: Identifying boundary with the whole closure in general is invalid

rules.name: Subspace topology rule
rules.output_form: open sets of Y are U intersection Y with U open in X
preconditions: Y is a subset of X with X already topologized
rules.operation: Induce the subspace topology by intersecting ambient open sets with the subset.
examples: Open intervals intersected with a subspace inherit subspace-open sets
counterexamples: Using arbitrary subsets of Y as automatically open in the subspace is invalid

rules.name: Product topology basis rule
rules.output_form: basis of products of open sets
preconditions: Factor topologies on X and Y are fixed
rules.operation: Generate the product topology from basic open products.
examples: Rectangles U x V with U and V open form a basis in X x Y
counterexamples: Taking arbitrary products of non-open subsets does not define basic open sets

rules.name: Homeomorphism criterion
preconditions: f and its inverse are continuous
rules.operation: Recognize topological equivalence through a continuous bijection with continuous inverse.
examples: Homeomorphic spaces have the same topology up to relabeling by a continuous bijection with continuous inverse
counterexamples: A bijection that is continuous but whose inverse is not continuous is not a homeomorphism

rules.name: Dense-set criterion
preconditions: A is a subset of the ambient space X
rules.operation: Characterize density through equality of closure with the ambient space.
examples: The rationals are dense in the real line under the standard topology
counterexamples: Merely being infinite does not imply density

rules.name: Nowhere-dense criterion
preconditions: A is a subset of the ambient space X
rules.operation: Characterize nowhere-dense sets by emptiness of the interior of their closure.
examples: Finite subsets of the real line are nowhere dense in the standard topology
counterexamples: A dense open set is not nowhere dense

rules.name: Baire category seed
rules.input_form: complete metric space or locally compact Hausdorff space
rules.output_form: countable intersections of dense open sets remain dense
preconditions: The space satisfies the standard Baire-category hypotheses
rules.operation: Use the Baire-category principle to preserve density under countable intersections of dense open sets.
examples: Baire category prevents a complete metric space from being expressed as a countable union of nowhere dense sets in the standard theorem setting
counterexamples: Applying the Baire conclusion outside the stated hypotheses is invalid

rules.name: Quotient topology definition
rules.input_form: surjection q: X -> Y and subset U of Y
rules.output_form: U open iff q^(-1)(U) is open in X
preconditions: q is the designated quotient map
rules.operation: Define quotient-space openness by preimages under the quotient map.
examples: Quotient spaces transport openness through the identifying surjection
counterexamples: Testing quotient openness by image preservation alone is invalid

rules.name: Continuous image of a compact space is compact
rules.input_form: continuous map f: X -> Y with compact X
preconditions: f is continuous
X is compact
rules.operation: Preserve compactness under continuous images.
examples: Continuous maps send compact intervals to compact subsets in their codomain topology
counterexamples: Dropping continuity invalidates the preservation claim

rules.name: Compact subset of a Hausdorff space is closed
rules.input_form: compact subset K of Hausdorff space X
preconditions: K is compact
X is Hausdorff
rules.operation: Combine compactness and Hausdorff separation to conclude closedness.
examples: Compact intervals in Euclidean spaces are closed because Euclidean spaces are Hausdorff
counterexamples: Assuming compact subsets are closed in arbitrary non-Hausdorff spaces is invalid

rules.name: Path connected implies connected
preconditions: For every two points in X, a continuous path joining them exists
rules.operation: Use path-connectedness as a sufficient condition for connectedness.
examples: Connected open intervals in the real line are path connected and therefore connected
counterexamples: Reversing the implication in general is invalid without extra hypotheses

rules.name: Finite product compactness rule
preconditions: The product topology is used
Only finitely many factors are involved
rules.operation: Preserve compactness across finite products.
examples: [0,1] x [0,1] is compact in the standard product topology
counterexamples: Replacing compactness by openness in the same statement is invalid

rules.name: Product Hausdorff rule
preconditions: The product topology is used
Only finitely many factors are involved
rules.operation: Preserve the Hausdorff property across finite products.
examples: Euclidean product spaces remain Hausdorff under the product topology
counterexamples: Claiming every product space is Hausdorff regardless of the factors is invalid

rules.name: Canonical form normalization expansion
preconditions: Auto-expansion rule requires explicit domain assumptions and validation metadata
rules.operation: Rewrite expressions into a canonical form that preserves the active equivalence relation.
examples: x + y and y + x map to a shared canonical additive form in commutative settings
counterexamples: Applying canonicalization rules outside their preconditions is invalid
common_errors: Using auto-generated rules without confirming domain-specific assumptions

rules.name: Substitution soundness expansion
rules.input_form: expression F(x) with admissible substitution x <- g
preconditions: Auto-expansion rule requires explicit domain assumptions and validation metadata
rules.operation: Substitute only under explicit domain and structural admissibility constraints.
examples: Replacing a variable by a constrained expression must preserve declared domain assumptions
counterexamples: Substitution that violates assumptions is invalid
common_errors: Using auto-generated rules without confirming domain-specific assumptions
